column1: What fundamental hardware tension drives nearly every architectural decision in a DBMS?
column2: RAM is fast but volatile, while disk is durable but slow. DBMS design (page size, buffer pools, WAL, transaction protocols) exists to reconcile this tension while handling concurrent access.

column1: Why does random I/O access without an index fail to scale, and by how much does sequential I/O outperform random I/O?
column2: Files are byte streams, so finding a specific record without an index requires scanning all preceding records. Sequential I/O outperforms random I/O by 100-1000x on spinning disk and 4-10x on NVMe SSDs.

column1: What atomicity guarantee does POSIX provide for the write(2) syscall, and why does this matter for databases?
column2: POSIX does NOT guarantee write(2) atomicity beyond a single filesystem block (typically 512B or 4KiB). This means concurrent writes can produce torn writes, requiring databases to implement their own consistency mechanisms (e.g., WAL) above the filesystem layer.

column1: In the multi-process database model (e.g., PostgreSQL), how do backend processes communicate and share state?
column2: Each client connection gets a dedicated forked OS process; all backends share a single large shared memory segment (buffer pool, WAL buffers, lock tables) coordinated via System V/POSIX shared memory and semaphores.

column1: What is the key crash-isolation trade-off between PostgreSQL's multi-process model and MySQL/InnoDB's multi-threaded model?
column2: In PostgreSQL's multi-process model, one backend crash does NOT bring down the server (hardware-enforced isolation via page tables). In MySQL's multi-threaded model, a single thread crash can corrupt or crash the entire process (software-enforced isolation only, no hardware boundary).

column1: What is the role of the PostgreSQL postmaster process?
column2: The postmaster is the supervisory process (PID 1 of the DB) that listens for incoming connections, forks a dedicated backend process per client, spawns background workers (checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher), and restarts crashed backends without affecting other connections.

column1: What is the core principle of Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)?
column2: Instead of overwriting data in place, each write creates a new timestamped version of the tuple. Readers see the most recent version committed before their snapshot timestamp, allowing readers and writers to proceed without blocking each other (snapshot isolation).

column1: What do the xmin and xmax fields represent in a PostgreSQL-style MVCC tuple header?
column2: xmin is the ID of the transaction that created (inserted) this tuple version. xmax is the ID of the transaction that deleted or superseded (updated) this tuple version; it is null/invalid if the version is still live.

column1: Under MVCC, when is a tuple version visible to a transaction T?
column2: A version is visible to T if its xmin committed before T's snapshot was taken, AND its xmax is either null/invalid or belongs to a transaction that committed after T's snapshot (i.e., the deletion hadn't happened yet from T's point of view).

column1: In MVCC, do writers acquire locks on individual tuple versions or on the logical tuple itself, and why does this matter?
column2: Writers acquire exclusive locks on the logical tuple (not individual versions). This prevents write-write conflicts while still allowing concurrent readers to access older versions without blocking, since reads never contend with the write lock.

column1: Why does MVCC avoid blocking readers against writers, unlike traditional locking concurrency control?
column2: Because readers operate on an immutable snapshot of previously committed versions rather than the current in-place row state, they never need to wait for a writer's exclusive lock on the logical tuple—write and read paths are decoupled.

column1: Explain the layered dependency hierarchy of a database system from hardware to application.
column2: Hardware Constraints → Storage Abstractions (pages, segments, files) → Concurrency Abstractions (locks, latches, MVCC versions) → Transaction Semantics (ACID) → Query Interface (SQL) → Application Logic. Each layer hides complexity from above and depends on guarantees from below; violations at lower layers (e.g., torn writes) corrupt all layers built on top.
